reasoning: The study generated new research data: PET imaging (11C-PBR28 and 18F-flortaucipir), MRI, neuropsychological testing, and neuropathology data from patients with svPPA and healthy controls collected specifically for this research, qualifying as D1 (Data Generated). For software, the paper used existing established research software tools like Freesurfer, PMOD, SPM12, and MATLAB curve fitting toolbox for processing and analysis, but did not develop or significantly extend any new software/algorithms - these are used as analysis tools (S2, Software Used).

The paper uses existing research software (SNANA for simulations, SALT2 light-curve fitter, PSNID classifier, CosmoMC, emcee) but develops its own BEAMS implementation and analysis code (made available on GitHub/Zenodo) - though this is an extension/application of the existing BEAMS method rather than claiming to create fundamentally new software, it's primarily using established tools like SNANA, SALT2, CosmoMC, emcee. The paper clearly generates substantial research data: they obtained 3147 new spectroscopic host galaxy redshifts via an extensive observational follow-up campaign using multiple telescopes (MMT, APO, WIYN, AAT), created 25 large-scale SNANA simulations (25,000+ simulated SNe), and generated new SN templates (added SN IIb and Ia-91bg templates to SNANA). This clearly constitutes generated research data (observational data and simulation outputs). Since data is generated, this falls into D1. For software, while they built on BEAMS and released their implementation code, the core analysis relies on established software packages (SNANA, SALT2, CosmoMC, emcee) without claiming significant new software contribution beyond applying/extending BEAMS methodology - this is best classified as S2 (software used) rather than S1.

The paper uses existing statistical software (R, package mgcv) for analysis - this is generic statistical software used as a tool, not developed/extended as a research contribution, so it falls under S2 (software used, not S3 since it's clearly research-oriented statistical modeling but still just utility use) - actually per criteria, R/mgcv are generic/established statistical packages, which could be S3. However they used GAM package mgcv which is more specialized than Excel but still an existing established package not created/extended by authors, so S2 (used) is appropriate rather than S1. For data, the study generated new experimental data (blood counts, genotyping, immunological assays) specifically for this research, collected from newly infested cattle - this constitutes generated research data (D1).

This is a conceptual/theoretical paper analyzing literature on bureaucracy and the Balanced Scorecard. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it collect, generate, or use research data (no empirical dataset, interviews, surveys, or simulations) - it purely synthesizes existing literature to build a conceptual framework.

This is a review/survey paper summarizing existing literature on energy storage for renewable-energy-driven water desalination systems. It does not report any new software development or use of computational tools, nor does it generate or use any research data (datasets, experiments, measurements). It synthesizes findings from other published studies without presenting original data collection, simulation runs, or software implementation. Hence it falls under No Software, No Data.

The paper uses existing research software tools (Weka, JADBio) for machine learning analysis without claiming to create or significantly extend these tools - classifying as S2 (Software Used). The paper generates new research data in two ways: (1) it analyzes an existing clinical dataset of 192 autism assessment cases, and (2) critically, it introduces and administers a novel autism screening questionnaire (ASTA) to new cohorts of patients (30 patients for first tool, 18 patients for second tool), collecting new survey/assessment data specifically for this research. This newly collected questionnaire data constitutes generated research data (D1), as the authors created new data through their own data collection instrument and clinical administration process, which goes beyond merely using a pre-existing dataset.

The paper implements its EMS using MATLAB and LABVIEW, both general-purpose software platforms used as tools (optimization solver, GUI/control implementation) rather than research software created or significantly extended for this work - this falls under "utility" use (S3). The paper does generate data: it creates simulation results (load/PV forecasts, BESS SOC curves, cost calculations) across four seasons, and conducts experimental verification on a laboratory microgrid producing real-time measurement data (power drawn, SOC curves, timing measurements). This generated data (simulation outputs and experimental measurement datasets) qualifies as D1 - research data generated through the study's experiments and simulations.

The paper collected raw sound/video recordings and survey/questionnaire data from 120 participants, generating new research data (soundscape samples, SQE and LoW evaluation responses), which is deposited in Mendeley Data - this qualifies as D1 (data generated). For software, the paper only used existing general-purpose tools (Adobe Audition CC for audio editing, SPSS for statistical analysis, Matlab for clustering analysis) as utilities to process/analyze data, not as a research contribution in itself, and no custom software/code was developed or claimed. This fits S3 (no research software).

The paper generated original behavioral observation data via CCTV monitoring of two binturong during zoo open/closed conditions, constituting newly created research data (D1). Software used was R (generic statistical software) and Microsoft Excel for data entry, which are generic tools not considered research software contributions, and no custom research software was developed or claimed as a contribution (S3).

This is a post-hoc secondary analysis of trial data from the SSaSS cluster randomised controlled trial. Data (cancer outcomes, participant records) were generated as part of the original trial but this paper uses that previously collected trial data for a new analysis, deriving statistics/findings from it—classified as data used (D2). No research software was created; the paper only mentions use of SAS, a generic statistical software package, which falls under "Generic statistical software" explicitly excluded as research software, so this is S3 (no research software).

The paper used established research software (SPM12/DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, 3D Slicer, SEEGA) but did not create or significantly extend any new software tools—these are existing packages applied to the data, so S2 applies. The study generated original research data: EEG-fMRI recordings, structural MRI scans, DCM model outputs, and connectivity results from 10 patients collected specifically for this study, which is clearly data generation (D1).

This is a narrative review article discussing and synthesizing findings from previously published GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on type 2 diabetes and cancer. The authors do not generate or use any research software themselves (no code, tools, or pipelines are described as part of this paper), nor do they generate or analyze any new research data—they simply summarize and interpret results reported in other published papers (citing statistics/findings from other studies rather than deriving them). Thus, there is no claim of software creation/use or data generation/use within this paper itself.

The paper develops a conceptual process-optimization model (lean-smart-green) and validates it through two real-world case studies (automobile and mining machinery shop floors). The authors collected production data (lead times, uptime, production per day, ergonomics issues, etc.) through Gemba walks, interviews, and brainstorming sessions, generating new observational/experimental data specific to these case studies (shown in Tables 2-5). This constitutes research data generation. However, no research software was created or used as a research contribution—the 'model' is a conceptual/methodological framework (workflow diagrams, strategic steps), not source code, scripts, or an implemented tool. Hence it is S3 (No Research Software) and D1 (Research Data Generated).

The paper uses existing panel survey data (Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey, RLMS) collected by others, which the authors analyze but did not generate themselves - this is D2 (data used). For software, they use standard econometric estimation methods (fixed-effects regressions, ordered logit with the 'feologit' Stata command by Baetschmann et al. 2020) - existing statistical packages/commands that are used but not created or significantly extended by the authors, which fits S2 (software used) rather than S1 (generated) or S3 (no software, since they explicitly cite using the BUC estimator command).

This is a purely theoretical linear algebra paper deriving matrix decomposition theorems and proofs. It uses a specific example matrix (the Wilson matrix) for illustration of theorems, but this is a well-known test matrix, not research data generated or collected through the research. No software was created or used (computations shown are manual/numerical examples, not claimed as software contributions). The paper explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article." There is no claim of generating or using research software or research data.

The paper uses an existing numerical model/code (described in Willis et al. 2007) for simulating rotating convection in the core, rather than claiming to have created new research software - the code is "available on request" but was developed in prior work, indicating software use (S2). The paper generates extensive new simulation data (an "extensive suite" of 68+ numerical simulations with varying parameters, Ra, E, q*) specifically for this study, representing newly created research data (model simulation outputs), which falls under D1 (Data Generated).

The paper uses existing publicly available long-read sequencing data (NABEC dataset, dbGaP/AnVIL accession) and derives findings/statistics from it, which qualifies as D2 (data used). The analysis relies entirely on established research software tools (Sniffles2, Napu pipeline, EMBOSS, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram) without claiming to create or significantly extend any new software - these are used as analysis tools, qualifying as S2 (software used).

The paper uses existing data on MERS-CoV cases among travelers, traveler volumes, trip lengths, and country populations (sourced from WHO, CDC, and other published data) to estimate cumulative severe case counts via a mathematical formula. No new research software is created or claimed—standard statistical/mathematical calculations (profile-likelihood CIs) are used as utilities, not as a software contribution. The data used (traveler case data, population data) is existing data derived from other sources, not newly generated by this study, and the paper's own output is a statistical estimate derived from this data rather than new data generation. Thus this is S3 (no software) and D2 (data used).

This paper involves field collection of shark specimens and copepod parasites, histological processing, and generation of new observational/histopathological data (histology slides, pathology descriptions, infection prevalence statistics) - this is newly generated research data. No research software is created or used (only standard lab equipment/processing like an autostainer, not research software), so it is S3. The data (histological specimens, slides deposited in museum, pathology observations) were generated as part of this study, making it D1.

The paper isolates and sequences 44 new flavobacterial phages, generating new genomic data (sequences, metagenomes, phage genome assemblies) - clearly D1 (research data generated). For software, the authors use a variety of existing bioinformatics tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLAST, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, ARB, RAxML, MiGA) but do not claim to have created or significantly extended any software package themselves; they only reference a "custom bioinformatics pipeline described elsewhere" which was published in a prior paper, not newly developed here. Thus this is S2 (software used, not generated in this paper).

The paper generates simulated/Monte Carlo data (synthetic data) under various model misspecification scenarios, which qualifies as D1 (data generated). For software, the authors use existing general-purpose statistical tools: R's "optim" function, the "NumDeriv" package for numerical derivatives, and the "ltm" R package for IRT model estimation. These are generic/existing research software packages used as utilities rather than software created or substantially extended by the authors, so this falls under S2 (software used) rather than S1. They also apply the methods to a real dataset (Detroit Area Study), but since data is generated via simulation, D1 takes precedence per the general rule that generated implies also used.

The paper describes the development of the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, an online software tool created by the authors (built under contract, with detailed methodology for scoring algorithms, biome-specific versions, etc.), which constitutes generated research software (S1). The paper also presents newly created data: the expert elicitation scores, judgement and evidence scores for actions and species groups across biomes, and example farm assessment data (before/after agri-environment scheme) that was compiled specifically for this research, constituting generated research data (D1).

The paper reports experimental synthesis and characterization of solid dispersions using PXRD, DSC, FTIR, and dissolution studies - generating new experimental data. No new research software was created; only standard commercial/instrument software (EVA, TA universal analysis, OMNIC) was used as utilities for data processing, which falls under S3 (software used only as utility, not a contribution).

This is a historical/architectural history paper using archival research (letters, exhibition catalogues, RIBA archives, press reports) as primary source data to construct an argument about Oliver Hill's exhibition design. It does not create or use any research software—no computational tools, models, or scripts are involved. It uses existing historical/archival data (letters, exhibition records, catalogues) that pre-existed the research, classifying it as D2 (data used, not generated). No software is claimed as generated or used (S3).

This is a scoping review that uses standard, widely-established tools (Excel worksheet, EndNote for deduplication, RoB2/ROBINS-I risk of bias tools) which fall under 'not research software' per the criteria - these are generic utility tools, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors. No novel research software was generated. The paper uses existing research data in the form of the included studies' data - it extracts, synthesizes, and tabulates data from 7 previously published clinical trials, compiling results into summary tables and risk of bias assessments. This constitutes using existing research data (findings/statistics derived from existing sources) rather than generating new primary research data, matching D2.

This crystal structure paper reports a newly synthesized compound and presents original crystallographic data (atomic coordinates, bond lengths/angles, hydrogen-bond geometry, CCDC deposition), which constitutes generated research data. The software used (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) are standard crystallographic analysis/refinement tools used but not developed or extended by the authors, so this is S2 (software used, not generated).

The paper generated new research data through interviews, focus groups, and a survey conducted as part of the project evaluation (interview transcripts, survey responses), qualifying as D1 (data generated). For software, NVivo was used for qualitative coding/analysis, which is a generic data analysis tool used as a utility rather than a research software contribution - but since it's a specific research software package (not general office software), it falls under S2 (software used) as there's no claim of creating or extending it, just using it as an analysis tool.

This is a literature review article that synthesizes and discusses existing published research on proteins in ionic liquids (keratins, collagens, silks, enzymes, etc.). The authors do not report generating any new experimental or computational data themselves, nor do they develop or use any specific research software as part of their own methodology - this is a narrative review compiling findings, data tables, and discussion from many previously published primary studies (citing solubility data, activity data, simulation studies, etc. from other researchers). Since the paper extensively uses/cites existing research data (solubility measurements, enzyme activity data, structural data, simulation results, tables of experimental literature values) to support its review and analysis, this falls under D2 (Data Used) rather than D1 (Data Generated), as no new data was created by the authors themselves. No software was generated or directly used by the authors in this work (it's a review, not a study involving computational tools employed by the authors), so this is S3 (No Software).

This is a qualitative case study based on interviews, non-participant observations, and archival/document research conducted by the authors over a longitudinal fieldwork period (2007-2014). The paper generates original research data (25 personal interviews, field observations, archival materials interpreted into case narratives) which constitutes newly created/generated research data. There is no mention of any research software being created or used (no computational tools, coding software, or applications discussed) - only qualitative interpretive analysis is described, which does not constitute research software use. Thus it is S3 (no software) and D1 (data generated through interviews/fieldwork).

The paper is an experimental physics study generating new data through optical measurements (PL spectra, ODMR, g2(τ) correlation measurements) on hBN defects - this constitutes generated research data (D1), even though it's only available 'upon reasonable request'. The paper does not describe creating or significantly extending any research software; analysis code is mentioned as available upon request but no claim of software development/contribution is made - code is used as a utility for curve fitting and simulations, not presented as a research contribution. Thus it falls under S3 (no software) and D1 (data generated).
